phase1.explanation:
Operators are how you actually DO something with the values sitting in your variables.

[[term:Arithmetic]] operators — `+ - * / %` — do what you'd expect, with one gotcha: [[warn:dividing two ints always gives you an int back, even if the real answer has a decimal]]. `10 / 3` is `3`, not `3.333`, because Java assumes if both sides are whole numbers, you want a whole number answer. `%`, the [[term:modulo]] operator, gives you the remainder instead — `10 % 3` is `1`.

[[term:Relational]] operators — `> < >= <= == !=` — compare two values and always hand back a `boolean`.

[[term:Logical]] operators combine booleans: `&&` (AND) needs both sides true, `||` (OR) needs at least one side true, and `!` (NOT) just flips whatever it's attached to.

And then there's the [[term:ternary operator]] — `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse` — really just an if-else squeezed onto one line. `(a > b) ? a : b` reads as "if a is bigger than b, give me a, otherwise give me b."

[[key:When operators start mixing together, parentheses aren't optional politeness — they're how you make sure Java evaluates things in the order you actually meant]].

phase2.errorMessage:
OperatorsExample.java:4: error: bad operand types for binary operator '+'
        System.out.println("a / b = " + a / b);
                                      ^
  first type:  String
  second type: int
phase2.explanation:
This is [[term:operator precedence]] biting you. `"a / b = " + a / b` doesn't read left-to-right the way you'd hope — `+` and `/` sit at the same precedence level, evaluated left to right, so it actually becomes `("a / b = " + a) / b`. And [[warn:you can't divide a String by an int]] — hence the error.

The fix is just parentheses: `"a / b = " + (a / b)` forces the division to happen first, THEN gets glued onto the string. [[key:Any time you're mixing arithmetic into a string with +, wrap the arithmetic in parentheses]] — it costs nothing and removes all ambiguity.

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Creates variables x=15, y=4
2. Prints: x + y = 19, x - y = 11, x * y = 60, x / y = 3, x % y = 3
3. Uses ternary to print which is bigger: "15 is bigger" or "4 is bigger"

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: `&&` and `||` are called short-circuit operators for a reason — if the left side of `&&` is already false, Java won't even bother checking the right side, since the answer's already decided. Same with `||` and a true left side. People rely on this to safely write things like `obj != null && obj.getValue() > 0`, where checking the right side first would crash.
